transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thanks. So, um, I guess I'm here because... well, things have been kind of weird lately. I'm 19, just taking some college classes, not really working right now, so I have a lot of downtime in my apartment, you know? And I've been having these, I don't know, moments with food. It's not just that I eat a lot sometimes, because, I mean, guys my age eat a ton, right? That's normal. But this is different. 

What really made me finally make the appointment and come in today is that... well, once I start eating like that, it's like my brain just disconnects. It literally feels like I hit some sort of switch in my head. I'll just keep going and going, eating whatever is in front of me, and the crazy part is, while I'm doing it, there's this rational part of my brain still awake. I'm literally sitting there thinking, Dennis, just stop already. You don't even want this anymore, just put the food down. But my hands just keep moving, and I keep chewing, and I just can't make myself stop. It's like I'm a passenger in my own body, just watching myself do this, and it's really starting to freak me out because I should be able to just stop when I want to, right? But I just keep going.
How do you feel after one of these eating episodes?

Oh, man... honestly? It's... it's just the worst feeling. The second that switch flips back and I actually realize what I just did, I just feel so incredibly embarrassed. And, um, just really grossed out with myself, to be completely honest. I'll look around at the wrappers or the empty containers on the counter, and I just sit there thinking, how did I just do that? 

And it's so frustrating because... well, usually, I'm a pretty disciplined guy, you know? Like, with my college classes, I always have my assignments done early, I map out my study schedule, I'm super organized with all my syllabi. And I do this robotics stuff, too, which takes a ton of focus and precision. You can't just lose control when you're coding or wiring a circuit, right? You have to be totally dialed in, and I *am* dialed in. I can sit for hours and just methodically work through a robotics build without losing my focus or messing up. 

So then, to go from being that guy—the guy who has his schoolwork perfectly scheduled and can build complex machines—to being this... this person who can't even stop himself from eating... it just makes me feel completely out of control. It makes me feel like I have absolutely zero control over my own self. And I hate that feeling. I just sit there in my apartment, looking at the mess, feeling completely disgusted and wondering why I can't just apply that same robotics discipline to, you know, eating a normal amount of food. It's just... it really messes with my head, honestly, because I should be better than that. I should be able to just be normal.
Do you feel guilty after these eating episodes?

Guilty? Yeah, I mean... yeah, definitely guilty. It's like, I'll be sitting there, right? And I've just finished, and the physical feeling is bad enough, but then the mental part hits. It's this overwhelming wave of, like, 'Dennis, why did you do that again?' And I just start mentally replaying the last, I don't know, twenty minutes, half hour, however long it was. And I think about all the moments where I could have stopped. Like, when I was walking to the kitchen, or when I opened the cabinet, or even when I was halfway through whatever I was eating. There are all these little decision points, right? And at every single one of them, I made the wrong choice. 

And that's where the guilt really comes from, I think. Because I know better. Like I was saying about the robotics and the schoolwork, I know how to make good choices and stick to a plan. But then I do this, and I just feel so guilty for letting myself down. I feel guilty for wasting the food, too, honestly. Like, I didn't even need it, I wasn't even hungry, and now it's just gone. And I'll think about, you know, my parents, and how they raised me to be responsible and not be wasteful, and I just feel like I'm failing at basic adulting. It's just this heavy, sinking feeling in my chest, and it lingers, you know? It doesn't just go away when I throw the wrappers in the trash. I'll carry that guilt with me for the rest of the day, sometimes even into the next day, just kind of beating myself up over it and promising myself I won't do it again, even though... well, even though I know I probably will. It's just exhausting, honestly, constantly feeling like I have to apologize to myself.
Do you enjoy the food while you're eating during these episodes?

Enjoy it? I mean, that's the thing... not really. Or, I don't know, maybe for the first bite or two, but honestly, it happens so fast that I don't even really taste it. It's almost like a blur. Like, normally, if I make myself a sandwich or something, I'll sit down, maybe put on a YouTube video about, you know, some new servo motor or whatever, and I'll actually eat it. But during these... these moments... it's completely different. 

I'll be standing there, like, right at my desk in my apartment. I have this whole setup, right? My laptop is open with my homework, and then I have my gaming monitor next to it, and I'll just be standing there between the two, just shoving food in my mouth. I don't even sit down. It's like I'm in this frantic rush, even though I have nowhere to be. I'll just be grabbing whatever—chips, cookies, bread, it doesn't even matter what it is—and I'm just eating it so incredibly fast. I'm barely even chewing, just swallowing and reaching for the next thing before I've even finished what's in my mouth. 

And because I'm eating so fast, I'm not enjoying it at all. I'm not savoring the flavor or thinking, 'Wow, this is really good.' It's just this mechanical, rapid-fire motion. Hand to mouth, hand to mouth, over and over. And then, suddenly, it's just... gone. Like, I'll look down, and a whole bag of something that should have lasted a week is just empty in a matter of minutes. And I'll think, 'Wait, did I really just eat all of that?' Because my brain didn't even have time to register the taste or the texture or anything. It's just this intense, high-speed consumption, and then it's over, and I'm just left standing there at my desk, feeling completely stuffed and realizing I didn't even get any pleasure out of it. It's just gone in a flash.
Do you feel like you're unable to stop eating once you start during these episodes?

Yeah... yeah, that's exactly it. That's actually the main reason I finally decided to make an appointment and come in here to talk to someone. Because it's like... it's like I hit some sort of internal switch, you know? Like a literal toggle switch in my brain just flips from 'normal Dennis' to whatever this is. 

Once I take that first bite, especially if it's something I wouldn't normally let myself have, it's just... I can't stop. I'll be standing there at my desk, like I said, just rapidly shoving food in, and there's this very clear, rational part of my brain that's still online. Like, the robotics guy part of my brain is sitting there watching this happen, and it's screaming, 'Dennis, just stop already! What are you doing? Put the bag down, step away from the desk!' 

But my hands just keep moving. It's the craziest feeling, like my body is completely disconnected from my brain. I'm literally watching my own hand reach into the bag of chips or the sleeve of cookies, and I'm telling myself to stop, but I just... don't. Or I can't. I don't know which it is, honestly. It's like a runaway train. Once it gets going down the track, you can't just throw the brakes on, even if you see the cliff coming. You just have to ride it out until it crashes. And that's what it feels like. I just keep going and going until either the food is completely gone or I physically feel so sick that my body forces me to stop. But yeah, the ability to just say 'okay, I've had enough, I'm going to stop now'? That is completely gone once that switch flips. It's terrifying, honestly, to feel that disconnected from your own actions.
Do you feel like you're in control of your eating during these episodes?

Control? No. No, not at all. That's... that's actually the whole thing. Like I was just saying, it's that feeling of being completely out of the driver's seat. It's the reason I'm sitting here right now, talking to you. Because if I had control, I wouldn't need to be here, right? I'd just tell myself to stop, and I would. But I can't. 

It's like I mentioned before, about that switch flipping. Once that happens, it's like my hands are on autopilot and my brain is just a passenger. I'll literally be standing there, between my laptop and my gaming monitor, just shoving whatever it is into my mouth, and there's this voice in my head—my own voice, just the rational, everyday Dennis voice—screaming at me. It's like, 'Dennis, what are you doing? Just stop already! Put it down! You don't even want this!' But it's like there's a disconnect between my brain and my body. The signal just isn't getting through. 

I can see myself doing it, I can hear myself telling me to stop, but the physical action just keeps happening. It's almost like watching a movie of yourself, you know? Like you're yelling at the character on the screen not to go into the dark basement, but they do it anyway because it's already in the script. I'm yelling at myself not to eat the rest of the sleeve of cookies, but my hand is already reaching for the next one. It's terrifying, honestly. To be a smart guy, a guy who understands how systems work, who builds robots and writes code and knows how to troubleshoot problems... and then to have a problem in my own system that I can't override. It just makes me feel so helpless. So, yeah, no control. None at all once it starts. It's just a runaway train until the food is gone or I feel sick.
Do you feel anxious or stressed before or during these eating episodes?

Anxious? Stressed? I mean... not exactly? Or, well, let me think about how to explain this. It's not like I'm sitting there sweating over a deadline or having a panic attack about an exam, you know? Like, I'm a sophomore, I'm taking some pretty heavy engineering courses this semester—thermodynamics, data structures, a really intense lab—and yeah, that stuff is stressful. But the eating... it doesn't really seem to map onto that. 

Like, I could be having a totally average Tuesday. I went to class, I came back to my apartment, I'm just sitting there at my desk with my dual monitors, maybe I'm just watching a stream on Twitch or looking at some code that isn't even due for a week. I'm not feeling particularly overwhelmed or anything. There's no big trigger, like a fight with a friend or a failed test. It's just... I'll just be there, and then suddenly the urge hits, and that switch I was talking about flips. 

And during it? No, I wouldn't call it anxiety. It's more like... like I said, it's frantic, it's a rush, but it's not because I'm stressed. It's just this intense drive to consume, this hyper-focused, mechanical thing. If anything, the anxiety only really comes *after*. That's when I start panicking, looking at the empty wrappers and thinking, 'Oh my god, what did I just do? How many calories was that? Why couldn't I stop?' That's when I feel stressed out and terrible about myself. But before or during? No, it's weirdly disconnected from my actual stress levels. It just kind of happens on its own schedule, regardless of what my mood is like.
Do you feel any relief after these eating episodes, even if it's temporary?

Relief? Oh, man. No. No, not even close. If anything, it's the exact opposite of relief. It's... it's honestly the worst part of the whole thing. 

Like, the second I stop—whether it's because the food is gone or because my stomach physically can't take another bite without me feeling sick—the reality of what just happened crashes down on me. It's immediate. There's no afterglow, no satisfaction, no 'oh, that hit the spot' feeling. It's just this immediate, crushing wave of embarrassment. I'll just be sitting there in my desk chair, looking at the empty family-size bag of chips or the crinkled up cookie wrappers, and I just feel so grossed out with myself. It's this deep, visceral disgust. 

And it's really hard for me to reconcile, you know? Because in literally every other aspect of my life, I am such a disciplined person. Like I was saying, I'm taking thermodynamics and data structures, I'm heavily involved in the robotics club, I write code... I'm a guy who thrives on logic and order and control. I plan my study schedules, I debug complex systems until they run perfectly. I know how to manage my time and my focus. So to go from being that guy—the guy who has his academic and extracurricular life completely locked down—to being a guy who just mindlessly shoveled thousands of calories into his mouth while staring blankly at a monitor... it's just so humiliating. 

It makes me feel like a total fraud, honestly. Like, how can I trust myself to build a functioning robotic arm when I can't even stop my own literal, biological arm from reaching into a bag of Doritos? It completely shatters this image I have of myself as someone who is in control. So, yeah, no relief. Just a ton of shame, a lot of self-loathing, and this horrible feeling that my brain is fundamentally broken in this one specific, completely irrational way. It's awful. It really is.
Do you think you would continue eating even if you weren't hungry during these episodes?

Hungry? I mean... I don't even know. I honestly haven't really noticed if hunger even plays a part in it at all. Like, I'm not really sure how to answer that because... well, it's like I was saying about the disconnect between my brain and my body, right? 

Normally, hunger is a very specific physiological response. Like, if I'm in my data structures lecture at 1 PM and I skipped breakfast because I was up late debugging some code for the robotics club, my stomach growls. I feel that physical emptiness, you know? It's a clear signal from my system saying, 'Hey, you need fuel.' But during these episodes? I couldn't even tell you what my stomach is feeling. It's like those sensors are just completely offline or being ignored by the main processor. 

I've never actually stopped in the middle of it all and asked myself, 'Dennis, are you actually physically hungry right now?' because the drive to eat doesn't feel like it's coming from my stomach at all. It's coming from somewhere else entirely. So, would I keep eating if I wasn't hungry? I really don't know, because I don't even know if I *am* hungry when I start. I could have literally just gotten back from the dining hall after eating a totally normal, filling dinner, and then an hour later I'm sitting at my monitors and that switch flips and I'm just consuming whatever is there. 

The physical sensation of hunger just seems completely irrelevant to the whole process. I'm not eating to satisfy a physical need, so whether that need exists or not doesn't seem to register. So I guess I just don't have a good answer for you on that one. It's just a totally blind spot for me when I'm in that state.
Do you ever make yourself vomit after one of these eating episodes?

Vomit? Oh, no. No, no, no. I've never done that. I mean, I know that's a thing people do, right? Like, you see it in movies or read about it online, people throwing up to get rid of the calories. But no, I don't do that. 

Honestly, the idea of throwing up is just... it's repulsive to me. I hate throwing up. Even when I'm actually sick, like if I catch a stomach bug or something, I will fight it for hours. I'll just lie there in bed, completely miserable, doing everything I can to not throw up because I just hate the physical sensation of it so much. It's so violent and out of control, you know? And like I've been saying, I'm a guy who really values control, even if I completely lose it during these eating things. 

Plus, mechanically speaking, it just seems like it would make the whole situation worse. Like, okay, I just had this horrible episode where I lost control and ate a ridiculous amount of food, and now I feel disgusting and ashamed. Making myself throw up wouldn't fix the fact that I lost control. It would just add another layer of grossness and physical discomfort on top of the psychological mess I'm already dealing with. It wouldn't reset the system, it would just crash it harder. 

And then there's the practical side of it. I live in a shared apartment. I have three roommates. We share two bathrooms. The logistics of trying to secretly throw up a massive amount of food without anyone hearing me or noticing... it's just not feasible. I'm already so embarrassed about the eating itself, I take all my empty wrappers out to the main dumpster behind the building at like 2 AM so my roommates don't see them in our kitchen trash. If they heard me throwing up, or if they figured out what I was doing... I couldn't handle that. The shame is already bad enough when it's just me in my room. Having other people know would be unbearable. 

So, yeah. No vomiting. I just sit there with the physical discomfort of being way too full, and the mental discomfort of knowing what I just did, and I just kind of ride it out. I'll drink some water, maybe take an antacid if my stomach is really burning, and just wait for the physical feeling to pass. But I never try to force it out. Never.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over time due to these eating episodes?

Weight changes? You know, that's actually the one variable in this whole messed-up equation that really doesn't make any sense to me. Because logically, if you look at the raw data, right? If you take the sheer caloric input of one of these... episodes... and you add it to my baseline metabolic rate, the output *should* be a massive increase in mass. It's basic thermodynamics, which is ironic since I was literally just talking about taking that class. Energy in, energy out, right? 

But... no. Not really. I mean, I haven't had to buy new jeans or anything. I step on the scale sometimes—we have one in the apartment bathroom, one of those smart scales that syncs to your phone, because my roommate Josh is obsessed with tracking his macros for weightlifting—and my weight graph on the app is basically just a flat line. There are some minor, totally statistically insignificant fluctuations, like maybe a pound or two depending on the time of day or whatever, but nothing major. 

I don't know if it's just because I'm nineteen and my metabolism is still running in high gear, or because our campus is huge and I'm constantly walking back and forth between the engineering quad and my apartment. Plus, I pace a lot when I'm trying to figure out a bug in my code... I can easily rack up like fifteen thousand steps on a Tuesday without even trying. So maybe my daily energy expenditure is just high enough to offset the surplus? Or maybe my body just doesn't process it all because it comes in such a concentrated, overwhelming burst? I really don't know. 

The math doesn't add up perfectly, which bothers me on a fundamental level, honestly. I hate when the numbers don't align. But physically, visually... no. I look exactly the same as I did when I started college. I haven't gained any noticeable weight. Which, honestly, almost makes the whole thing easier to hide, you know? Like, if I was gaining thirty pounds, my parents or my roommates would notice and probably say something. But because my weight is completely stable, it's just this invisible, messed-up routine running in the background that nobody else can see.
Do you think these eating episodes are triggered by your emotional state?

Emotional state? I mean... that's a really tough variable to quantify, honestly. When you say emotional state, my mind immediately goes to the cliché, you know? Like what you see on TV, where someone goes through a horrible breakup or gets fired from their job, and they're sitting on the couch crying and eating a whole tub of ice cream. But that's not... that's not really what this is for me. 

I don't really feel particularly emotional before it happens. Or at least, I haven't noticed any kind of consistent emotional pattern. I mean, sure, I get stressed. I'm a sophomore engineering student taking eighteen credit hours this semester, including this algorithms class where the professor grades on a curve that is honestly just statistically cruel. So yeah, there's baseline stress. I'm anxious about my GPA, I'm constantly thinking about whether my resume is good enough to land a decent internship next summer, and I don't sleep as much as I probably should. But is that stress actually triggering the eating? I really don't know. 

Because the thing is, I've tried to map it out. I actually sat down a few weeks ago and tried to look for a correlation, like, okay, did I have a massive project due the day after an episode? Was I feeling particularly down or anxious? But the data is just completely all over the place. There's no clear pattern. I've had episodes on a Tuesday night when I'm pulling my hair out over a compiler error, but I've also had them on a totally relaxed Saturday afternoon when I literally have nothing to do and I'm just hanging out in my room feeling perfectly fine. Sometimes I'm stressed, sometimes I'm bored, sometimes I'm actually in a really good mood because I just aced a quiz. 

And when the actual eating starts, it's not like I'm eating *at* my emotions, if that makes sense. Like I said before, it's more like a disconnect. My brain just goes into screensaver mode. The emotions, whatever they are at that moment, just kind of get suspended or muted. So I honestly couldn't tell you if an emotion is the catalyst, because I don't feel a spike in sadness or anger or even anxiety right before I start eating. It just sort of... happens. It's like a subroutine that just starts running in the background without any clear input command. So, yeah, I really haven't noticed any specific emotional trigger. I wish I had, because then at least I'd have a root cause to troubleshoot, but right now, I just don't know.
Do you criticize yourself after these episodes for losing control over your eating?

Oh, man. Yeah. The self-criticism is... it's probably the loudest part of the whole process. Once the actual eating stops, and that sort of mental screensaver mode I mentioned finally turns off, reality just comes crashing back in. And it hits hard. I'll look around at the empty wrappers, or I'll just feel that heavy, uncomfortable physical weight in my stomach, and I just feel so incredibly embarrassed. It’s this intense, overwhelming feeling of being just completely grossed out with myself. It’s hard to even articulate how disgusted I get. 

And I think the reason it hits me so hard, the reason I beat myself up so relentlessly over it, is because it's just so completely contradictory to who I am in literally every other aspect of my life. Like, I’m an engineering student, you know? I'm on the university robotics team. That stuff requires an insane amount of precision and discipline. When we're coding a microcontroller for a robot, every single line of code has to be intentional. You have to account for every variable, every edge case, because if you don't, the whole system fails. I apply that exact same level of discipline to my coursework. I map out my study schedules in spreadsheets, I track my deadlines... I am a person who runs on logic, structure, and control. 

So then, to have this one area of my life where I just completely short-circuit and lose all of that discipline? It makes absolutely no sense to me, and it makes me feel like I’m completely not in control. And for someone like me, feeling out of control is basically my worst nightmare. I sit there afterward and I just tear myself apart mentally. I'll literally be sitting on the edge of my bed thinking, "How could you let this happen again? You're smart enough to program an autonomous navigation system, but you can't stop yourself from eating a family-sized bag of chips and a whole sleeve of cookies?" 

It just feels like a massive system failure that I can't debug, and the fact that I can't fix it makes me criticize myself even more. The lack of control is just... it's fundamentally unacceptable to me. So yeah, I definitely criticize myself. I just sit there feeling gross and ashamed, over-analyzing the whole thing and hating that I let it happen.
Is guilt the main emotion you feel right after these eating episodes?

Guilt... I mean, I guess guilt is definitely a part of the equation, sure, but like I was kind of just saying a minute ago, it's really more about being embarrassed. And just... feeling completely grossed out with myself. 

Because, you know, when I think of the word guilt, I usually think about, like, doing something wrong to someone else? Like, if I forgot to push my code to the shared GitHub repository and my robotics team missed a competition deadline because of me, I'd feel guilty. I'd feel like I let the team down. But this... this is entirely internal. It’s this heavy, uncomfortable embarrassment. I’ll just look at the aftermath, the wrappers or whatever, and feel so incredibly grossed out by my own actions. 

And it really all stems from that contrast I was just talking about. I'm usually so incredibly disciplined with everything else in my life. Between my engineering classes, my rigid study schedules, the robotics lab... my whole life is built on structure and being completely in the driver's seat. We have these strict protocols in the lab where you document every single iteration of a design, and it's all about maintaining absolute control over the environment and the variables. So to suddenly have this one thing happen where I just... don't have that discipline at all? It makes me feel like I’m completely not in control of my own hardware, if that makes sense. 

And for me, losing control is just the absolute worst possible feeling. It's a total system failure. So, yeah, I guess guilt is in the same emotional family, but if we're being precise about it, the main things are definitely the embarrassment, feeling grossed out, and just hating that I'm not in control.
Do you notice these eating episodes happening more often after a particularly stressful or emotional event in your life?

Well, like I was kind of touching on earlier when we were talking about emotional states... I really haven't seen a spike in frequency after a specific event, either. I know it seems like it should work that way, right? Like basic cause and effect. A big stressful event happens, the system gets overloaded, and boom, an episode. But the data just doesn't support it. 

For instance, just to give you a concrete example, a few weeks ago we had the regional qualifiers for our robotics team. I'm the lead for the autonomous navigation module, and our collision-avoidance sensors were completely bugging out literally two days before we had to pack up and travel. I was pulling 16-hour days in the lab, practically living on black coffee, and the stress was just... it was off the charts. My heart rate was probably elevated for 48 hours straight. You'd think that would be the prime time for an episode, right? If it was tied to a stressful event, that would be the absolute peak of the graph. But... nothing. I didn't have an episode at all. 

But then, fast forward to a week later. The competition is over, we actually placed second, the pressure is completely off. I'm literally just sitting in my dorm folding laundry on a random Thursday afternoon. No exams the next day, no immediate deadlines, nothing. And out of nowhere, my brain just shifts into that screensaver mode I mentioned, and it happens. 

So, yeah, I've really tried to isolate the variables here. I even thought about setting up a spreadsheet at one point to track my daily stress levels on a scale of one to ten against the occurrence of these episodes, just to see if maybe there was a delayed reaction? Like, maybe there's a lag in the system where the stress of an event hits me two or three days later and causes a crash. But honestly, even looking back at it informally, I just can't find a trend line. It’s incredibly frustrating because, as an engineer, I want to find the root cause so I can patch the bug. But whether I just survived a massive physics midterm or I'm just having a completely unremarkable weekend, the frequency doesn't seem to change at all.
Do you feel like these episodes are a result of you giving in to cravings or a complete loss of control over your actions?

Cravings? No, no, it's definitely not just a craving. I mean, everyone gets cravings, right? Like, you're in the lab late and you think, "Man, I could really go for some pizza." That's a normal craving. You can choose to order the pizza, or you can choose to just drink some water and go to sleep. You still have agency. You're still making a choice. 

But this... this is entirely different. It’s absolutely a complete loss of control. Honestly, that's the core issue here. What really made me come in, what finally made me realize I needed to actually talk to someone about this, is that once I start eating like that, it feels like I hit some switch and I just keep going. It's like an automated sequence gets initiated and the manual override is completely disabled. 

And the craziest, most frustrating part of the whole thing is that my logical brain is still awake while it's happening. I'm completely aware. I'll just be sitting there, continuing to eat, and there's this rational part of me trapped inside, watching it happen, and I'm thinking, "Dennis, just stop already." Like, I am literally telling myself, "You don't even want this, just put the wrapper down, abort the process." But my hands just keep moving. It’s like a ghost in the machine. I’m actively telling my body to stop, but the physical hardware just completely ignores the command line. 

So, yeah, if it were just a craving, I could logic my way out of it. I'm good at logic. But when that switch flips, my logic doesn't matter at all. It's a total, terrifying loss of control, and that's why I'm here. Because I can't figure out how to rewire that switch.
Do you think these episodes might be related to a specific emotional state, such as feeling sad, anxious, or bored?

Specific emotional state... right. Sad, anxious, bored... well, I mean, I've really tried to analyze this from every angle, like I was saying before with the stress thing. I've tried to map it out. And you'd think, logically, there would be a correlation, right? Like, sadness equals episode. Boredom equals episode. But honestly... no. I really can't tie it to any specific emotional state at all. 

I mean, I've had episodes when I was feeling totally fine. Like, I remember one time a couple of months ago, I was actually in a great mood. We had just finally debugged this really tricky bit of code for the robot's arm articulation, and I was feeling super accomplished, you know? Just... happy. Relaxed. I went back to my room, threw on a podcast, and then suddenly... boom. The switch flips. And then, on the flip side, I've been incredibly anxious—like when I thought I was going to fail my differential equations midterm—and nothing happened. No episode. 

And boredom? I mean, I guess I have some downtime, but usually I'm so busy with classes and the lab that I don't really have time to be bored. But even when I do have a free afternoon, like that laundry day I mentioned, it's not like I'm sitting there feeling this crushing sense of ennui that drives me to eat. It's just... it's like my brain just checks out. It goes into that screensaver mode. But it's not a *feeling*, if that makes sense? It's not an emotion. It's an absence of input. 

I've even tried to keep a journal about it, you know? Just a little notebook where I jot down what I was feeling right before it started. I figured if I could just identify the trigger emotion, I could build a workaround. Like, "Okay, Dennis, you're feeling anxious, time to go for a run instead." But the entries are just all over the place. "Felt fine." "Tired." "Thinking about physics." "Happy." There's no pattern. It's completely random noise. And as someone who spends his life looking for patterns and optimizing systems, having this completely unpredictable variable just dropping in whenever it feels like it... it's maddening. It really is. So, yeah, long story short, I haven't been able to link it to sadness or anxiety or boredom or anything else. It just... happens.
Do you feel like you're giving in to cravings when these episodes happen or is it more like you've lost control over what you're doing?

Wait, didn't we just... I mean, I know I kind of went off on a tangent about this a few minutes ago, but yeah, to reiterate, it's absolutely the loss of control. Not cravings at all. Like I was saying, that total loss of control is the exact thing that really made me come in to see you in the first place. 

Because it's terrifying, honestly. I can't stress that enough. Once I start eating like that, it feels like I hit some master switch, and the automated sequence just takes over, and I just keep going. And I'm fully aware while it's happening, which is the absolute worst part of the whole experience. Part of me is trapped in there, wide awake, thinking, "Dennis, just stop already. You don't need this, just put the food down." But I can't do it. It's like my physical body has completely muted my rational brain's administrative privileges.

I sit there afterward and I just tear myself apart mentally. I'll literally be sitting on the edge of my bed thinking, "How could you let this happen again? You're smart enough to program an autonomous navigation system, but you can't stop yourself from eating a family-sized bag of chips and a whole sleeve of cookies?" 

It just feels like a massive system failure that I can't debug, and the fact that I can't fix it makes me criticize myself even more. The lack of control is just... it's fundamentally unacceptable to me. So yeah, I definitely criticize myself. I just sit there feeling gross and ashamed, over-analyzing the whole thing and hating that I let it happen.

patient.answer:
Guilt... I mean, I guess guilt is definitely a part of the equation, sure, but like I was kind of just saying a minute ago, it's really more about being embarrassed. And just... feeling completely grossed out with myself. 

Because, you know, when I think of the word guilt, I usually think about, like, doing something wrong to someone else? Like, if I forgot to push my code to the shared GitHub repository and my robotics team missed a competition deadline because of me, I'd feel guilty. I'd feel like I let the team down. But this... this is entirely internal. It’s this heavy, uncomfortable embarrassment. I’ll just look at the aftermath, the wrappers or whatever, and feel so incredibly grossed out by my own actions. 

And it really all stems from that contrast I was just talking about. I'm usually so incredibly disciplined with everything else in my life. Between my engineering classes, my rigid study schedules, the robotics lab... my whole life is built on structure and being completely in the driver's seat. We have these strict protocols in the lab where you document every single iteration of a design, and it's all about maintaining absolute control over the environment and the variables. So to suddenly have this one thing happen where I just... don't have that discipline at all? It makes me feel like I’m completely not in control of my own hardware, if that makes sense. 

And for me, losing control is just the absolute worst possible feeling. It's a total system failure. So, yeah, I guess guilt is in the same emotional family, but if we're being precise about it, the main things are definitely the embarrassment, feeling grossed out, and just hating that I'm not in control.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was kind of touching on earlier when we were talking about emotional states... I really haven't seen a spike in frequency after a specific event, either. I know it seems like it should work that way, right? Like basic cause and effect. A big stressful event happens, the system gets overloaded, and boom, an episode. But the data just doesn't support it. 

For instance, just to give you a concrete example, a few weeks ago we had the regional qualifiers for our robotics team. I'm the lead for the autonomous navigation module, and our collision-avoidance sensors were completely bugging out literally two days before we had to pack up and travel. I was pulling 16-hour days in the lab, practically living on black coffee, and the stress was just... it was off the charts. My heart rate was probably elevated for 48 hours straight. You'd think that would be the prime time for an episode, right? If it was tied to a stressful event, that would be the absolute peak of the graph. But... nothing. I didn't have an episode at all. 

But then, fast forward to a week later. The competition is over, we actually placed second, the pressure is completely off. I'm literally just sitting in my dorm folding laundry on a random Thursday afternoon. No exams the next day, no immediate deadlines, nothing. And out of nowhere, my brain just shifts into that screensaver mode I mentioned, and it happens. 

So, yeah, I've really tried to isolate the variables here. I even thought about setting up a spreadsheet at one point to track my daily stress levels on a scale of one to ten against the occurrence of these episodes, just to see if maybe there was a delayed reaction? Like, maybe there's a lag in the system where the stress of an event hits me two or three days later and causes a crash. But honestly, even looking back at it informally, I just can't find a trend line. It’s incredibly frustrating because, as an engineer, I want to find the root cause so I can patch the bug. But whether I just survived a massive physics midterm or I'm just having a completely unremarkable weekend, the frequency doesn't seem to change at all.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's eating episodes are related to a sense of loss of control
doctor.question: Do you feel like these episodes are a result of you giving in to cravings or a complete loss of control over your actions?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: What really made me come in is that once I start eating like that, it feels like I hit some switch and I keep going even while part of me is thinking, Dennis, just stop already.

patient.answer:
Cravings? No, no, it's definitely not just a craving. I mean, everyone gets cravings, right? Like, you're in the lab late and you think, "Man, I could really go for some pizza." That's a normal craving. You can choose to order the pizza, or you can choose to just drink some water and go to sleep. You still have agency. You're still making a choice. 

But this... this is entirely different. It’s absolutely a complete loss of control. Honestly, that's the core issue here. What really made me come in, what finally made me realize I needed to actually talk to someone about this, is that once I start eating like that, it feels like I hit some switch and I just keep going. It's like an automated sequence gets initiated and the manual override is completely disabled. 

And the craziest, most frustrating part of the whole thing is that my logical brain is still awake while it's happening. I'm completely aware. I'll just be sitting there, continuing to eat, and there's this rational part of me trapped inside, watching it happen, and I'm thinking, "Dennis, just stop already." Like, I am literally telling myself, "You don't even want this, just put the wrapper down, abort the process." But my hands just keep moving. It’s like a ghost in the machine. I’m actively telling my body to stop, but the physical hardware just completely ignores the command line. 

So, yeah, if it were just a craving, I could logic my way out of it. I'm good at logic. But when that switch flips, my logic doesn't matter at all. It's a total, terrifying loss of control, and that's why I'm here. Because I can't figure out how to rewire that switch.

patient.answer:
Specific emotional state... right. Sad, anxious, bored... well, I mean, I've really tried to analyze this from every angle, like I was saying before with the stress thing. I've tried to map it out. And you'd think, logically, there would be a correlation, right? Like, sadness equals episode. Boredom equals episode. But honestly... no. I really can't tie it to any specific emotional state at all. 

I mean, I've had episodes when I was feeling totally fine. Like, I remember one time a couple of months ago, I was actually in a great mood. We had just finally debugged this really tricky bit of code for the robot's arm articulation, and I was feeling super accomplished, you know? Just... happy. Relaxed. I went back to my room, threw on a podcast, and then suddenly... boom. The switch flips. And then, on the flip side, I've been incredibly anxious—like when I thought I was going to fail my differential equations midterm—and nothing happened. No episode. 

And boredom? I mean, I guess I have some downtime, but usually I'm so busy with classes and the lab that I don't really have time to be bored. But even when I do have a free afternoon, like that laundry day I mentioned, it's not like I'm sitting there feeling this crushing sense of ennui that drives me to eat. It's just... it's like my brain just checks out. It goes into that screensaver mode. But it's not a *feeling*, if that makes sense? It's not an emotion. It's an absence of input. 

I've even tried to keep a journal about it, you know? Just a little notebook where I jot down what I was feeling right before it started. I figured if I could just identify the trigger emotion, I could build a workaround. Like, "Okay, Dennis, you're feeling anxious, time to go for a run instead." But the entries are just all over the place. "Felt fine." "Tired." "Thinking about physics." "Happy." There's no pattern. It's completely random noise. And as someone who spends his life looking for patterns and optimizing systems, having this completely unpredictable variable just dropping in whenever it feels like it... it's maddening. It really is. So, yeah, long story short, I haven't been able to link it to sadness or anxiety or boredom or anything else. It just... happens.

Wait, didn't we just... I mean, I know I kind of went off on a tangent about this a few minutes ago, but yeah, to reiterate, it's absolutely the loss of control. Not cravings at all. You don't need this, just put the food down." But I can't do it. It's like my physical body has completely muted my rational brain's administrative privileges. 

So, yeah, it's definitely a complete loss of control, not just me giving in to wanting a snack. If it were just a normal craving, I wouldn't be here taking up your time, you know? But this is a complete system override, and no matter how much I'm yelling at myself internally to stop, I just keep going until it runs its course.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's episodes are more aligned with Other Specified Feeding or Eating Disorder (F50.8) or Unspecified Feeding or Eating Disorder (F50.9) based on the presence of purging behaviors

patient.answer:
Purging? Like... throwing up, or taking pills? No. No, I've never done anything like that. I mean, I know that's a thing people do, like bulimia, right? But no, that's not me. I've never made myself throw up. The thought of it actually really grosses me out, to be honest. I hate throwing up. Even when I've had the flu or whatever, I'll do anything to avoid it. 

And laxatives or diuretics? No way. I'm pretty careful about what I put in my body, generally speaking—well, outside of these episodes, obviously. But I don't like taking medication unless I absolutely have to. I don't even like taking ibuprofen for a headache if I can just drink water and wait it out. So taking pills to... what, flush my system? That just seems like adding another chaotic variable to a system that's already malfunctioning. It doesn't make logical sense to me to try and fix one extreme behavior with another extreme behavior. 

As for excessive exercise... I mean, what counts as excessive? I'm not a gym rat or anything. I don't go run a marathon after an episode. Sometimes, if I'm feeling really physically uncomfortable—like, if my stomach is physically stretched and hurting from eating so much—I might go for a walk around the campus just to try and get things moving, you know? Just to relieve the physical pressure. But it's not like a punishment. It's not like I'm calculating the calories I just consumed and trying to burn them off on a treadmill. It's purely just... mechanical relief, I guess you could call it. 

Usually, honestly, after an episode, I'm just so exhausted. It's like my body diverted all its power to processing the food, and my brain is just drained from the whole internal battle. I mostly just want to lie down and sleep, or at least zone out. The idea of going to the gym and doing a high-intensity workout right after eating like that... I think I'd probably pass out. Or actually throw up, which, like I said, I really don't want to do. So, no, none of that stuff. I just eat, and then I deal with the aftermath, usually by just feeling terrible about myself and trying to sleep it off.
